ghk-cu.text: Users apply GHK-Cu, and some inject it in peptide blends, to improve skin texture, fine lines, acne scars and hair density. It is promoted as a skin-and-hair peptide in looksmaxxing circles. Evidence is mostly topical cosmetic studies; the injectable use rests largely on anecdote.

matrixyl.text: Matrixyl is a cosmetic peptide used in serums and creams that users apply to soften wrinkles and fine lines, including around the eyes. It is marketed as a collagen-boosting ingredient. Small studies, mostly manufacturer-linked, have measured modest wrinkle changes.

argireline.text: Users apply Argireline as a needle-free alternative to Botox for forehead lines and crow's feet. It is marketed as "topical Botox" because it imitates part of a protein botulinum toxin targets. Studies are small and short, and skin penetration is a debated question.

snap-8.text: SNAP-8 is used in serums and eye creams by people aiming to soften forehead and eye-area expression lines, and is described as a stronger relative of Argireline. Claims of Botox-like effects come mainly from manufacturer data; independent human trials are scarce, and injectable versions are discussed only on forums.

carnosine.text: Carnosine is taken orally or applied in skincare by users who want to slow skin aging, based on the idea that it limits sugar damage to collagen. Forum posters also include it in supplement stacks. Evidence for skin appearance in people is limited; most data are lab or animal studies.

spironolactone.text: Spironolactone is a prescription antiandrogen and diuretic. Appearance-focused users take it, or apply it topically, for hormonal acne, and some also discuss it for DHT-related hair loss, body hair and water retention. Acne use in women is clinically studied; hair, puffiness and male use are largely off-label and anecdotal, with feminizing side effects noted.

clascoterone.text: Clascoterone is a topical antiandrogen cream that users apply to the skin for acne without systemic hormone effects. It is also being investigated for androgenetic hair loss, which draws interest from hairline-focused users. Acne use is approved and trial-backed; hair use is still under study.

pdrn-polynucleotides.text: PDRN or polynucleotide "skin boosters" are injected or applied by people seeking skin rejuvenation, scar improvement and recovery after lasers or microneedling. They are popular in Asian dermatology clinics. Some clinical studies exist for wound healing and skin quality; evidence for cosmetic uses is smaller and varies by product.

omega-3-epa-dha.text: Users take fish oil for its anti-inflammatory effect, hoping for clearer skin, less puffiness, better hair and generally better recovery. It is a common baseline supplement in appearance forums. Trials exist for inflammation and some skin conditions; direct appearance effects are less well studied.

chain: Mineral supports skin and immune function
zinc.text: Users take or apply zinc for inflammatory acne, redness, and hair shedding tied to deficiency, and some link it to testosterone, beard or voice claims. Evidence exists for acne and deficiency-related hair loss; the hormone, voice and height claims are anecdotal. It is also discussed alongside GHK-Cu because of copper balance.

chain: Calorie deficit and lower body fat
semaglutide.text: Users take semaglutide to lose body fat quickly, which also slims the face and reduces puffiness. Forum posters also discuss "Ozempic face" hollowing and muscle loss. Weight loss is well studied in trials; the facial effects are reported anecdotally and in case discussions rather than measured.

tirzepatide.text: Users take tirzepatide to cut body fat, often claiming it works better than semaglutide, with the face leaning out as weight falls. Trials show large weight loss in people with obesity. Appearance outcomes such as facial leanness or muscle retention are untested and based on anecdote.

liraglutide.text: Liraglutide is a daily GLP-1 injection that users discuss as an older, milder fat-loss option than semaglutide. It is used to cut body fat. Weight-loss effects are studied in trials; claims about muscle sparing or dosing around cravings are anecdotal.

retatrutide.text: Retatrutide is an investigational drug that users source as research peptides, hoping for the largest fat loss yet and sometimes stack with TRT or anabolics. Trials report large weight loss but it is unapproved. Use for body recomposition and the equivalence of vials to trial drug are untested.

cagrilintide.text: Cagrilintide is an experimental amylin analogue that users discuss alone or with semaglutide as a strong appetite suppressant for getting lean. It is in clinical trials and unapproved on its own. Fat loss is studied in trial populations; looks-focused "leanmaxxing" claims are opinion.

chain: Less hunger in rare genetic obesity
setmelanotide.text: Setmelanotide is approved only for obesity from rare genetic pathway disorders, so its appearance link is indirect: it is mentioned in fat-loss peptide discussions. Its weight effects are studied in those specific patients; use for ordinary fat loss in otherwise healthy people is untested.

tesamorelin.text: Tesamorelin is a prescription GHRH analogue that users, often with ipamorelin, take to lose fat and raise IGF-1. It is approved for abdominal fat in HIV lipodystrophy. Use in healthy people for physique or facial leanness is off-label and largely anecdotal.

aod-9604.text: AOD-9604 is a growth hormone fragment sold as a research peptide that users take for fat loss without GH side effects, often stacked with other peptides. It was tested for obesity in humans with disappointing results. Its looks-related effects are claimed mainly on forums.

hgh-fragment-176-191.text: HGH Fragment 176-191 is sold as a research chemical and discussed in bodybuilding forums as a way to mobilize fat like growth hormone without its growth effects. Users stack it with secretagogues or stimulants. Evidence is preclinical; human fat-loss data are lacking.

5-amino-1mq.text: 5-Amino-1MQ is a gray-market small molecule that users take to raise fat metabolism and lose body fat. It is not a peptide, despite how it is sold. Evidence is limited to cell and animal studies; human fat-loss and safety data are absent.

chain: Less fat gain, better nutrient partitioning
berberine.text: Berberine is a plant alkaloid users call "nature's metformin", taking it to cut body fat, improve nutrient partitioning during bulks, and sometimes calm acne. Trials show modest effects on glucose, lipids and weight. Acne and partitioning claims are largely anecdotal.

l-carnitine.text: Users take L-carnitine as a fat burner and recovery aid, sometimes injected. It is promoted for shifting fat into energy use. Trials show small and inconsistent weight effects in most healthy people; injected versions and recovery claims rest mainly on anecdote.

chain: Green tea catechin raises metabolism slightly
egcg.text: EGCG is a green tea extract that users take as a fat burner, often before workouts, and some speculate about muscle effects via myostatin. Studies show small thermogenic effects with mixed results. The muscle-building claim is based on lab findings and anecdote.

capsaicin.text: Capsaicin from chili peppers appears in fat-loss diets and supplements, where users take it for a small metabolic and appetite boost. It is also tied to lip plumping and facial leanness discussions. Human studies show slight effects on energy use; the appearance claims are anecdotal.

creatine-monohydrate.text: Users take creatine to train harder and build muscle and strength, and it is a baseline supplement in physique-focused circles. Its muscle and strength effects are among the best studied of any supplement. Claims that it causes hair loss via DHT or kidney damage are debated and less well supported.

whey-protein.text: Users take whey to hit protein targets, build muscle, and support leaner physiques while dieting. Muscle gain from adequate protein is well studied. Some forum posters link whey to acne, an association that has some observational support but limited controlled trials.

leucine.text: Users add leucine to drinks or meals because it triggers muscle growth signaling, and compare protein sources by leucine content. Acute signaling is well studied; whether extra leucine beyond adequate protein adds measurable muscle is less clear.

beta-alanine.text: Beta-alanine is a pre-workout ingredient users take to get more work from high-rep sets, which they expect to translate to more muscle. It is studied for high-intensity performance gains. Direct effects on muscle size are less established; the tingling is a known harmless side effect.

hmb.text: HMB is used by lifters wanting to preserve muscle during cuts and recover faster, and is sometimes called a steroid alternative. Studies show benefits mainly in untrained or older people or during illness; effects in trained lifters are mixed and the steroid comparison is unsupported.

chain: Boosts nitric oxide and blood flow
citrulline-malate.text: Users take citrulline malate in pre-workouts for a muscle pump and more reps, and some pair it with tadalafil for blood flow. Studies on reps and endurance are mixed, and the pump's effect on long-term muscle growth is untested.
